newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania faces chaos without political compromise.
newsitem.headline: Albania faces chaos without political compromise.

text.p: Albania will be thrown back into chaos if political parties cannot reach a compromise over arrangements for a general election, a group of European politicians said on Monday.
Leaders from the Council of Europe's Parliamentary Assembly said there seemed to be a chance for Albania's political parties to reach a package of compromises so the poll could proceed on June 29.

However, Albanian President Sali Berisha's refusal to compromise over citizens' committees, set up in some towns as Albania slid towards anarchy in March, was a stumbling block in talks. He insists they are disbanded before the election.

"If there was to be no election...it means chaos for Albania," Jaakko Laakso, a Finnish member of the United European Left, told a news conference after two days of talks by the European politicians in the capital Tirana.
"It concerns the salvation and fate of Albania to have elections now."
Peter Scheider, of the Socialist Group, said a compromise package seemed possible from all the parties involved in an interim multi-party government.
"The only person who did not see a chance to reach such a package and was clearly against it was the president," said Scheider, an Austrian.
"It must be one of the jobs of the parties to convince the president."

Prime Minister Bashkim Fino, a Socialist, heads the nine-party interim government that was formed on March 9. Its right-wing Democratic Party predecessor resigned amid a wave of violence over the collapse of popular, high-risk savings funds.
To stop the slide towards chaos, Berisha agreed to appoint the interim government and call a fresh election.
This calmed passions among Albanians still smarting from a poll last May, described by international observers as seriously flawed, which gave the Democrats a landslide victory.

But the Democrats and the Socialists have to agree on a list of issues. These include the number of seats to be decided by proportional representation, constitutional changes, and the treatment of citizens' groups or salvation committees, which sprang up as law and order disintegrated.

Some Albanian politicians see the committees as bridging the gap before local governments, the police and army resume control. Others say the committees are run by armed, criminal gangs with political motives, making a free and fair poll impossible.
"I think it is critical...these bands are disbanded," said Norwegian Hallgrim Berg, of the European Democratic Group.
Parliament has to agree on the proposed election by May 15 for the poll to be able to proceed on June 29.

"It has become progressively clearer..that the way in which these committees are to be dealt with is likely to be the critical issue," said Briton Sir Russell Johnston, of the Liberal, Democratic and Reformers group.
"It seems to us in the other important areas -- the election law, the question of the genocide law, the question of television time for the election -- compromise is possible."
Fino and the other party leaders in the interim government were due to meet later on Monday to continue discussions.
